title: How do you solve an operations case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete operations case guide: mapping a process, finding the bottleneck with simple maths, worked through hospital emergency waiting times.
hook: You solve an operations case by following the work from start to finish, measuring time, cost and errors at each step, and finding the one step that holds everything up: the bottleneck. Fix that step first, prove the effect with simple capacity maths, then check which step becomes the new constraint. This guide works through a hospital emergency department and an outpatient clinic, with every number shown.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet an operations case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example: emergency waiting times
  • Capacity maths: proving the bottleneck
  • Strong and weak answers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Practise with these prompts
  • Where to practise next

When you will meet an operations case

Something is too slow, too costly or too error-prone: waiting times have doubled, a factory cannot meet orders, deliveries are late, a process needs too many people. Operations cases are common in public sector, healthcare, manufacturing and logistics work. They overlap with cost cases, but the focus is one process and how work flows through it, rather than the whole cost base.

The structure, and the first question to ask

Ask which outcome matters, because the fixes differ:

Which outcome matters most here: cost, speed, capacity or quality? And is anything off limits, such as safety standards or headcount?

Then use three layers:

  • Map it. The steps and hand-offs; time, cost and errors at each step; where work queues up.
  • Fix the steps. Eliminate, combine, re-order or simplify (often called ECRS). Technology often does the simplifying.
  • Fix what supports them. People (skills, incentives, staffing by hour) and systems.

One principle drives the whole case: the slowest step sets the output of the whole process. Speeding up any other step adds nothing, so fix the bottleneck first. The process framework covers each layer in more depth.

A fully worked example: emergency waiting times

The prompt: a hospital's emergency department waiting times have doubled in a year. Why, and what should it do? The data below is illustrative.

Step 1: map the flow

Follow a patient: arrive, triage, see a doctor, tests, decision, then either go home or be admitted to a ward bed upstairs.

Step 2: rule out the obvious

Arrivals are up only 5% and staffing is unchanged. A 5% rise in demand does not explain waits doubling, so the cause is probably inside the process or at its exit.

Step 3: look at the exit

About 300 patients arrive a day and a quarter of them, 75, need a ward bed. Wards mostly discharge patients late in the afternoon, so admitted patients now wait about 6 extra hours in the emergency department for a bed to free up.

Step 4: put a number on it

75 patients × 6 hours = 450 cubicle-hours a day. Divided by 24 hours, that is like having about 19 cubicles permanently blocked by patients who have already been treated. New arrivals have nowhere to be seen, so everyone waits.

Step 5: size the fix

If moving ward discharges earlier in the day cuts the wait for a bed from 6 hours to 2, blocked capacity falls to 75 × 2 ÷ 24 ≈ 6 cubicles. That frees about 12 to 13 cubicles, far more than the department could gain by hiring.

Step 6: the recommendation

The bottleneck is not the emergency department itself but beds upstairs: admitted patients occupy the equivalent of 19 cubicles while they wait. I'd move ward discharges earlier in the day, open a discharge lounge so patients can wait for transport off the ward, and work with social care on patients ready to go home. Cutting the bed wait to two hours frees about 12 cubicles. Extra emergency staff alone would not fix it. I'd pilot this on two wards and track bed-wait times and emergency waits weekly.

Capacity maths: proving the bottleneck

A simple calculation often settles the argument. An outpatient clinic has two stages:

StageStaffTime per patientCapacity per hour
Nurse intake3 nurses15 minutes3 × 4 = 12
Doctor consultation2 doctors20 minutes2 × 3 = 6

If 8 patients arrive each hour, the doctor stage can see only 6, so the queue grows by about 2 patients every hour. Hiring another intake nurse changes nothing, because intake is not the constraint. Two fixes work:

  • Add capacity at the bottleneck. A third doctor lifts consultation capacity to 9 an hour, above the 8 arriving.
  • Reduce demand on the bottleneck. Safely routing 25% of visits to a nurse-led pathway cuts demand on doctors from 8 to 6 an hour.

Notice the catch in the second fix: demand of 6 against capacity of 6 means doctors are 100% busy. Real arrivals and appointment lengths vary, so queues still build at full utilisation. Saying so shows real operational judgement. Both fixes also assume enough rooms and support staff, and the nurse-led route must be clinically safe. Once you fix one bottleneck, ask which step becomes the next one.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer reaches for resources:

Waits are long, so the hospital should hire more doctors and nurses for the emergency department.

A strong answer follows the work and quantifies the constraint:

Let me follow a patient from arrival to leaving and see where the time goes.
Admitted patients waiting for beds tie up the equivalent of 19 cubicles. Speeding up any other step adds nothing until we fix that.

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Asking for more staff first. Check where the delay actually happens before adding resources.
  2. Analysing every step equally. Find the bottleneck and spend your time there.
  3. Not putting a number on it. "19 cubicles blocked" persuades; "beds seem to be an issue" does not.
  4. Fixing a step that is not the constraint. It makes one team look busier and changes nothing for the customer.
  5. Forgetting variability. A process run at 100% of capacity on average will still have queues.

Practise with these prompts

Quick maths: a bottling line fills 1,200 bottles an hour, caps 900 and labels 1,000. What is its output, and what happens if you speed up capping to 1,100?

Show the answer

Output is 900 an hour, set by capping. Speed capping up to 1,100 and output rises only to 1,000, because labelling becomes the new bottleneck. The extra 100 an hour of capping capacity is wasted unless labelling is also improved.

A parcel company's on-time delivery fell from 95% to 85%.

Show the answer
  • Where in the chain: collection, sorting hub, trunk transport between hubs, last mile. Which step has the delays?
  • Volume against capacity: parcel growth against vans, drivers and sorting hours; peaks by day and season.
  • Process and systems: route planning, scanning, missed hand-overs; any new system or hub recently?
  • External: weather, traffic, partner carriers, address and access problems.

Where to start: locate the step where parcels start running late.

The trap: listing causes without locating where in the chain the delays start.

An airline's aircraft spend 20% longer on the ground between flights than rivals'.

Show the answer
  • Arrival: waiting for a gate, stand or tug; taxi times.
  • Aircraft servicing: cleaning, catering, fuel, bags. Which task is on the critical path?
  • Boarding: boarding process, cabin bags, late passengers.
  • Planning: schedule buffers, crew connections, ground staff at peak times.

Where to start: the critical path, the longest chain of steps that must happen one after another. Speeding up steps off that chain does nothing.

The trap: trying to speed up every task when only those on the critical path matter.
